promptHtml: A self-checking testbench checks every cycle the same way. Follow one value of d through dff_tb, from the moment the testbench sets it until it has been checked. Put these in order.
explanationHtml: The flip-flop and the model both act at the rising edge, so they are compared half a cycle later, at the falling edge, when both hold their new values (lesson 3.3). Only a difference prints and counts. The verdict comes once, after the last cycle.
steps: `next_cycle` sets `d` to a new value, just after a falling edge.
At the rising edge, the flip-flop and the model both take that value.
At the next falling edge, `next_cycle` compares `q` with the model's `d_at_edge`.
If they differ, it prints TEST FAILED with the time and adds 1 to `errors`.

promptHtml: This is the reference model in two_flops_tb, the testbench of lesson 2.2's two flip-flops in a row: q1 is d one cycle late, and q2 is d two cycles late. d1 models q1, and d2 models q2. Type the missing line, without its semicolon.
explanationHtml: d2 <= d1; makes d2 take, at each rising edge, the value d1 had just before it: d two cycles late, as q2 should be (lesson 2.2). A model is the behaviour written the simplest way you can trust (lesson 3.3). Use <= here, as in every clocked block (lesson 2.2): d2 = d1; would happen to work, because the line above still uses <= and has not changed d1 yet, but with = on both lines d2 would read the new d1, and the model would be a single flip-flop.

promptHtml: dff_tb must print TEST PASSED only if no check failed. Type the condition.
explanationHtml: Each failed check adds 1 to errors, so errors == 0 means none failed (lesson 3.3). errors is a count, never X, so == is enough here. A testbench that printed TEST PASSED without this test would pass a broken design.
before: // Testbench for dff. It drives d with a fixed pattern and, after every
// rising edge, checks that q equals the value d had at that edge.
logic d_at_edge;  // the value d had at the most recent rising edge
// A 10 ns clock (100 MHz, like the Arty A7's oscillator).
// Rising edges at 5, 15, 25 ns and so on; falling edges at 10, 20, 30 ns.
// What a D flip-flop must do: remember d at each rising edge.
// Wait for the next falling edge, check q, then set d for the next cycle.
// Changing d on falling edges keeps it steady at every rising edge.
// clk starts as X, and X to 0 counts as a falling edge, so wait for a
// real rising edge before the first falling one (D96).
// Part 1: d changes only on falling edges.
// Part 2: a short pulse on d that starts and ends between two rising
// edges. The flip-flop never sees it.
#2 d = 1'b1;  // 2 ns after the falling edge...
#2 d = 1'b0;  // ...and gone 1 ns before the next rising edge

promptHtml: This is the testbench of lesson 1.1's 4-bit adder, which has no clock: each step sets a and b, waits 10 ns, then checks. Type what it works out as the right five-bit sum.
explanationHtml: The testbench's own model of the adder is a + b, put into the five-bit expected, so no carry is lost (lesson 1.1). It then compares low with the bottom four bits and carry with the top one, using !==. A design with no clock is checked after a fixed wait instead of at a falling edge, but the idea is the same (lesson 3.3).
before: // Testbench for adder4. Each step sets a and b, waits 10 ns, then checks
// low and carry against the sum the testbench works out itself.
logic [3:0] a, b;       // the inputs the testbench sets
logic [3:0] low;        // the outputs it checks
logic [4:0] expected;   // the five-bit sum this step should give
int         errors;     // how many steps went wrong
// One step: set a and b, wait 10 ns, then compare.
task automatic step(input logic [3:0] va, input logic [3:0] vb);
after: $display("TEST FAILED: %0d + %0d gave low=%0d carry=%b at %0d ns",
// Part 1: numbers from 0 to 9, which look the same in hexadecimal.

promptHtml: This should be lesson 0.2's alarm: siren is 1 when the alarm is armed and the door or the window is open. Its self-checking testbench first prints TEST FAILED: 010 gave siren=1, expected 0 at 20 ns, where the three digits are armed, door_open and window_open. Pick the line that is wrong.
explanationHtml: The failing row has armed at 0 and the door open, and the siren sounds, which it must not do while the alarm is off. armed | opening is 1 when either is 1; the alarm needs armed & opening, 1 only when both are. The line for opening is right: the door is open, so opening should be 1. A TEST FAILED line that names the inputs, the value and the value expected leads you straight to the line to read (lessons 0.4 and 3.3).
